one_liner: C++-native deep learning framework from FAIR (wav2letter successor) that trains standard networks slightly faster than PyTorch 1.8 and TensorFlow 2.4.
what_it_does: A full training framework written in C++: tensors (fl::Tensor), tape-based autograd (fl::Variable), nn modules (fl::Module, Sequential, Conv2D, Transformer and others), optimizers, distributed data-parallel training, plus domain packages and apps for speech recognition, image classification, object detection and language modelling. You write models in C++ against its own API and link the CMake target flashlight::flashlight; it is not a drop-in for PyTorch or TensorFlow code, and the Python bindings for the core were removed (only the separate flashlight/text and flashlight/sequence packages ship Python).
how_it_is_fast: The default tensor backend is ArrayFire, which JIT-fuses chains of element-wise ops into generated kernels; convolutions and RNNs go to cuDNN (or oneDNN on CPU), and with benchmark mode on, fl::DynamicBenchmark times the candidate cuDNN algorithms online and keeps the fastest. A caching block allocator (CachingMemoryManager: 512-byte rounding, 2 MiB small-block and 20 MiB large-block pools, block splitting) is installed as the default memory manager, and multi-GPU gradient sync uses a coalescing all-reduce (CoalescingReducer over NCCL). The rest of the edge is low framework overhead: no Python interpreter in the training loop, which is why the gap is largest on small, overhead-bound models such as AlexNet.
when_to_use: You need to train or fine-tune networks inside a C++ application or service with no Python runtime at all.

Research on framework internals: adding a custom tensor backend through fl::Tensor (subclass TensorAdapterBase and TensorBackend), custom memory managers or new autograd ops, in a core of roughly 20k lines.
Small or launch-overhead-bound models where per-op framework overhead dominates (the paper's AlexNet rows: 1.4 s vs 2.0 s PyTorch on 1 GPU, 2.1 s vs 6.0 s on 8 GPUs per 100 iterations).
Speech recognition work that builds on the wav2letter lineage (ASR app, CTC and ASG criteria, beam-search decoding via flashlight/text) on Linux with NVIDIA GPUs.
when_not_to_use: Large standard models where the paper shows only 1-18% gains over the faster of PyTorch 1.8 and TensorFlow 2.4 (derived from page data) and TensorFlow wins VGG16 on 1 GPU; current PyTorch releases were never compared, so there is no evidence it is faster today.
Python-first teams or anyone needing the PyTorch/TensorFlow ecosystem (pretrained models, model import, torch.compile, recent attention kernels): none of these appear in the files read.

Windows, macOS beyond a minimal OpenCL core build, or AMD GPUs: the vcpkg ports declare !(windows | osx), Windows build issue #1181 and ROCm request #1099 are open, and the README requires a Linux-based OS.

CPU-only small MLPs: issue #898 (2022) reports the Perceptron example much slower than JAX+Flax with jit on CPU, and issue #630 (2021) reports ResNet-34 training on V100 slower than PyTorch; no maintainer replies or fixes were visible on either page.
Projects that need upstream support: an open 'Future of Flashlight' issue (#1185, Nov 2025) says PRs are not reviewed, and recent commits are automated Meta fbcode syncs and build fixes.

integration.form: static lib (shared with BUILD_SHARED_LIBS), consumed as the CMake package flashlight::flashlight; also vcpkg ports flashlight-cuda and flashlight-cpu
integration.dependencies: ArrayFire >= 3.7.3 (one of its CUDA, CPU or OpenCL backends) for the default tensor backend; CUDA >= 9.2 with cuDNN (and NCCL for distributed) on GPU, or oneDNN >= 2.5.2 with gloo on CPU; an MPI library for distributed training (required by all apps); cereal and stb; a BLAS (Intel MKL or OpenBLAS) for flashlight/lib; gflags and glog for apps; libsndfile and flashlight/text for ASR
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.16 (top-level CMakeLists; README still says 3.10); README says C++17 with gcc >= 7, but main uses std::unordered_map::contains (C++20) in fl/runtime/DeviceManager.cpp, so a strict C++17 build fails (issues #1183 with g++ 11.4, #1187); CUDA code is compiled as C++14
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA) or CPU (oneDNN or ArrayFire CPU); macOS only as a minimal ArrayFire-OpenCL core build; no Windows vcpkg support; no ROCm

gotchas: Harness bug in the repo's own benchmark (flashlight/app/benchmark/Run.cpp, runDetr): targetBoxes and targetClasses are constructed with batchsize default (empty) Variables and the generated targets are then push_back'ed after them, while HungarianMatcher::compute reads indices 0..batchsize-1; it therefore sees 12 empty targets, takes its 'targetClasses.isEmpty()' shortcut and never builds a cost matrix or runs the Hungarian solve. The README's DETR throughput rows (21.64 img/s FP32 on 1 V100) do not include real set-matching work. This affects only that Flashlight-only table, not the paper's PyTorch/TensorFlow comparison, whose scripts are not public.

The paper measured Flashlight 0.3.1 (pre fl::Tensor rewrite, ArrayFire-only era); v0.3.2 is described as the last release before the fl::Tensor breaking changes, and main (0.4.0 in CMakeLists, with new JIT and oneDNN tensor backends) is different code. The vcpkg ports pin the 0.3 branch tip, so vcpkg users get the old API, not the one in the README examples.

The repo's benchmark tool uses synthetic fl::rand inputs reused every iteration (no data loading), 50 warm-up plus 100 timed updates, and an fl::sync() after each of forward, criterion, backward and optimizer step, so its throughputs are not comparable with the paper's data-loading-inclusive times.
There is no Python API for the core library: bindings/python now only points to flashlight/text and flashlight/sequence.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Flashlight over OneFlow or LightSeq when you want a whole training framework that lives entirely in C++ and whose internals you intend to modify; OneFlow offers a PyTorch-like Python API with a public multi-framework DLPerf harness, and LightSeq accelerates Transformer layers inside existing PyTorch training. Pick it over llm.c when you need many architectures (CNNs, ViT, DETR, ASR and LM Transformers) rather than one hand-written GPT-2 training path.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' ICML 2022 paper (Table 3, read only through search-result snippets because arXiv and PMLR are blocked here) times 100 forward-plus-backward iterations including data loading for AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet-50, a BERT-like Transformer, an ASR Transformer and ViT on a DGX-1 (Intel E5-2698, V100-32GB) with Flashlight 0.3.1 vs PyTorch 1.8 and TensorFlow 2.4. Flashlight is fastest in 11 of 12 rows, but outside AlexNet (1.43x on 1 GPU, 2.86x on 8 GPUs vs PyTorch) the margin over the faster competitor is 1.01x to 1.18x, and TensorFlow wins VGG16 on 1 GPU (12.6 s vs 13.2 s) (ratios derived from page data); compiler, flags and the baseline scripts are not published.
status_note: Commits are recent (2026-10-06; CUDA 13 nvToolsExt fix 2026-09-14), but they are automated Meta fbcode syncs and lint or build fixes rather than feature work; the last tagged release is v0.3.2, and issue #1185 (Nov 2025) says PRs go unreviewed. It is MIT-licensed and usable, but expect to fix build problems yourself (C++20 use despite the C++17 claim, outdated NCCL in vcpkg #1186).
